name: Bubble tea shop
blurb: Open a boba shop or kiosk selling milk tea, fruit tea and toppings
title: Bubble Tea Shop: How to Start a Boba Shop Business
description: How to start a bubble tea shop or boba shop business: how it makes money, the lease, permits and equipment, franchise traps, who it suits and how to test first.
h1: How to start a bubble tea shop
answer: A bubble tea shop sells made-to-order milk teas, fruit teas and toppings such as tapioca pearls from a shop, kiosk or stall. Ingredients are cheap per cup, but rent, staff and fit-out are not, and many shops are franchises with fees and supply rules that tie you in, so the lease and the contract decide most of the outcome.

sections.h: How a boba shop makes money
body: Customers pay per drink, with extra for toppings, larger sizes and add-ons. Delivery apps add sales but take a commission.

Costs include rent, staff, tea, milk, syrups, pearls, cups and sealing film, utilities, equipment upkeep, delivery-app fees and, for franchises, royalties and required supplies. Pearls and fresh ingredients have a short life, so waste matters.

ul: A site with steady foot traffic, often near schools, malls or transit, under a lease you have read carefully.
Equipment: sealing machine, pearl cooker, fridges, shakers, water filtration and a point-of-sale system.
Permits and food safety: rules differ by country and city. Examples include a business licence, food premises registration or permit, health inspection and food handler training.
Recipes and suppliers, or a franchise agreement that supplies them.
Staff who can make drinks fast and consistently at peak times, and insurance.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who know drink trends and their local crowd
Anyone without savings for a lease and fit-out
Owners willing to work the counter in the early months
People who want a hands-off investment
Sites with students, shoppers or commuters
Streets already crowded with similar shops

ul: Rent: many first shops fail because takings never cover the lease.

Franchise fees, royalties and required supplies; in the US, the FTC says franchisors must give you their disclosure document at least 14 days before you sign or pay, and suggests talking to current owners.
Competition: boba shops often cluster, and a new one nearby can split your trade.
Seasonality and weather, especially for cold drinks.
Buying an existing shop: verify sales with bank records and check the remaining lease.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Map boba and tea shops near your target street and note prices and queues.
Make your menu at home and get honest feedback from people who drink bubble tea often.
Sell at a market stall or pop-up, where food rules allow, to test prices and demand.
Get quotes for rent, fit-out and equipment for one candidate site.
Work out the cups per day needed to cover rent and staff; stop if that number looks unrealistic.
Have a lawyer read the lease and any franchise contract before signing.
Get food permits, inspections and insurance in place.
Launch a short menu and train staff on recipes and speed.
List on maps and delivery apps, and check the commission against your margin.
Track cups sold, waste and best-selling drinks daily, and trim the menu.

faq.q: Should I open a franchise or an independent boba shop?
faq.a: A franchise gives you a brand, recipes and supply, but you pay fees and royalties and must follow its rules. An independent shop is more flexible but you build everything yourself. Read the full franchise disclosure and talk to current owners before deciding.

faq.q: Can I start with a kiosk or stall?
faq.a: Often yes, and it lowers rent and fit-out costs. You still need food permits, and a kiosk depends heavily on foot traffic at that spot.

faq.q: What is the biggest cost in a bubble tea shop?
faq.a: For most shops, rent and staff, not the ingredients. Check those numbers for your site before anything else.
